extracted.intended_audience: college students and scholars of American government and public policy; state policymakers and administrators
extracted.subtask_short: state regulation of industry and labor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes state statutory and administrative standards for regulating common carriers, banking, insurance, and labor (hours, safety, compensation, bureaus, mediation) in early 20th-century American law and policy. Useful as a reference for understanding legal requirements and administrative practices states employed to control corporations and protect workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and statistical reporting by railway companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Each railway company is required to maintain a public office and publish from time to time statistics relative to its business, profits, dividends, transfer of stock, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is public record and transparency; forms part of state supervision to allow assessment of rates and corporate conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and passenger-convenience obligations for railroads
rubrics_metrics.description: Railroads are compelled to maintain fences, regulate grade crossings, put in switches under certain conditions, adopt safety appliances, heat and light their cars, and do many other things for the safety and convenience of passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates the scope of positive regulatory duties imposed on common carriers to secure passenger safety and comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical valuation of railroad property for rate control
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions must ascertain reasonable value of the property of the carrier, amount expended in construction and equipment per mile, cost to secure right of way, cost to reconstruct roadbed/track/depots/transportation facilities, and amount required to replace physical properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a basis for allowance of income for investment and for apportioning earnings between state and interstate traffic; detailed accounting (bonds, indebtedness, proceeds, sales) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed accounting of corporate indebtedness and transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission must ascertain outstanding bonds, debentures, indebtedness (amount, when issued, rate, when due, purposes), to whom issued or sold, price received, use of proceeds, holders of indebtedness, floating indebtedness, credits, property on hand, judicial sales and amounts purportedly paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of physical valuation and financial transparency enabling regulators to judge fairness of rates and corporate decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative powers of public service/corporation commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions are empowered to inquire into general condition and management of all common carriers; examine books and papers; investigate accidents; fix rates and services; order repairs and improvements to secure adequate services; order changes in time schedules; inspect gas and electric meters and fix gas and electric rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad supervisory authority varying by state; used to adapt regulation where positive enactment cannot foresee all operational details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on corporate transfers and issuance without commission approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Common carriers cannot assign, transfer, or lease franchises, acquire stocks and bonds of other common carriers, or issue stocks, bonds, or other evidences of indebtedness without the approval of the commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls corporate consolidation and financial maneuvers that might affect service, rates, or competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of rates and prohibition of unfair practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Common carriers must keep open for public inspection their schedules showing rates and fares and charges; they must grant no rebates or unjust discrimination or unreasonable preferences; they must grant no free passes except to certain specified persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public access to rate schedules plus prohibitions on rebates and preferences aim to ensure fair and uniform treatment of customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and enforcement for violations of commission orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations are enforced by drastic penalties: every day's violation constitutes a separate and distinct offense, involving a penalty of $5000 for common carriers and $1000 for corporations other than common carriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High statutory fines and daily penalties provide strong enforcement incentives; amounts are illustrative of early-20th-century statutes cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition, appointment, and removal of commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public service commissions usually consist of from three to five members — in the eastern states generally appointed by the governor and in the West and South frequently elected by popular vote; members removable by the governor 'for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or misconduct in office' after charges and an opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets institutional design and accountability mechanisms for administrative regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banking supervision and periodic examination requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: State superintendent of banks is charged to examine, personally or through competent examiners, every bank and trust concern at least twice each year and every savings bank at least once in two years, inquiring into conditions and resources, mode of conducting business, investment of funds, safety of management, and security afforded to engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent, thorough examinations intended to make deposits as safe as government bonds; part of comprehensive consolidated banking law.

rubrics_metrics.name: State deposit-guarantee funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states (e.g., Oklahoma) require banking institutions to contribute to a state fund used to guarantee depositors so that in case a bank fails depositors may look to the state for repayment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism to protect depositors and enhance public confidence; an early form of deposit insurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance corporation regulation and supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: State insurance codes provide for detailed regulation of every form of insurance under supervision of a state superintendent of insurance charged with making periodical examinations into the conduct of insurance corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel to banking supervision — periodic oversight to protect policyholders and ensure solvency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory hours on public works and special-hour legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states have established a compulsory eight-hour day for labor on public works; constitutions or statutes may permit regulation and fixation of wages, hours of work, and protections for persons employed by the state or contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes special constitutional provisions for mines/smelters and other hazardous employments; state-by-state variation is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of hours for specific occupations including rail employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws have fixed maximum hours for conductors, engineers, firemen, telegraph/telephone operators, and train dispatchers (examples: maximums of sixteen or fourteen hours per day in some states); a federal statute limited hours of railway employees to sixteen per day for interstate commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap of state and federal rules; federal law yields where state establishes a lesser maximum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional constraints on hours and labor legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws regulating hours must take into account principles applied by the federal Supreme Court in protecting private rights; some statutes (e.g., NY bakery hours law) have been declared unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative design must consider due process and property rights limits recognized by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special protections for women and limits on their hours/night work
rubrics_metrics.description: About one-half of the states have limited hours of labor for women in important branches of industry; some laws forbid employment of women between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. in textile manufacturing establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-level variation in hours and protective provisions, often tending toward ~60 hours per week historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child-labor prohibitions, hour limits, and education requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly every state prohibits employment of children under a certain age in factories, limits hours for children above the age limit, forbids night work for children, and generally fixes minimum age around fourteen with requirement of a minimum of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes a critique that arbitrary age limits may be inferior to physical-capability tests; emphasizes enforcement and variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage-fixing commissions and minimum wages for women and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions may be established to fix wages of women and children in industries; if commission finds wages too low it may set up a wage board to ascertain a minimum wage and request the employer to pay it; refusal may be published but not punished by penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative remedy centered on inquiry and publicity rather than direct penal enforcement in some states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mothers' pensions for widows with small children
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws provide for mothers' pensions to widows who have small children and do not have means for support; amounts are customarily graded by number and age of children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-welfare measure aimed at preventing institutionalization of children and preserving family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace safety, sanitation, and equipment standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws require ventilation of factories/workshops, safeguarding dangerous machinery, penalties for unsafe scaffolds/ladders, regular inspection and maintenance of elevator cables/gears, provision of fire escapes for factories over three stories, suitable meal times, periodic boiler examinations, prohibition of laundry work in living rooms, cleanliness of laundries and bakeries, restrictions on tenement-house manufacturing, and mine ventilation/timbering/suitable outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad set of prescriptive health-and-safety standards intended to reduce accidents and unsanitary conditions; enforcement varies and often lags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of enforcement gaps and comparative international lag
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many prescriptive labor and safety laws exist, the United States is often behind advanced European nations and the laws are frequently not enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as normative observation guiding calls for stronger administration and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of negligence-based employers' liability system
rubrics_metrics.description: The negligence-based system is criticized as fundamentally wrong in principle, failing to remedy social problems, involving waste (high legal costs), embittering employer-employee relations, and being morally demoralizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical rationale for adopting compulsory workmen's compensation and shifting away from fault-based suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for employer responsibility and cost internalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should bear the cost of indemnifying victims of industrial accidents because accidents are frequently due to the nature of the industry; the cost should be treated as a normal item of production expense borne by consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic and social justification for compulsory compensation and insurance schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workmen's compensation and state insurance schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory or voluntary compensation schemes require employers to pay injured workmen fixed amounts regardless of fault; some states established state insurance plans funded by employer contributions; constitutional amendments and statutory designs were used to meet judicial objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York enacted a compulsory law (later declared unconstitutional by state court), Washington adopted a state insurance plan, other states used constitutional amendments to authorize laws; UK model imposes compensation according to fixed scale except for wilful misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory abrogation of fellow-servant defense in hazardous industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states (e.g., Oklahoma) expressly abrogate the common-law fellow-servant doctrine as to every employee of every railroad company, street railroad company, interurban railroad company, and every concern engaged in mining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative removal of a traditional employer defense to expand employee recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law standards for recovery under certain state laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Under some laws (e.g., New York in 1910), only an employee who exercised due care and whose injury was due to defects in machinery for which the employer or his agents were responsible could secure damages; entering a business implied assumption of 'necessary risks' after due care by employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates limits on recovery under negligence regimes and contrasts with compensation models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation and duties of labor bureaus and inspection services
rubrics_metrics.description: States have established labor bureaus and factory inspection to enforce labor laws regarding hours and wages and to maintain sanitary standards; duties include appointing a labor commissioner, inspecting factories and mines, collecting statistics of labor/manufactures/accidents, and sometimes administering employment offices and mediation/arbitration laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor bureau is an important administrative branch; appointments are often political, leading to tenure instability; bureaus coordinate nationally via conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of free public employment offices and associated concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states have made provision for free public employment offices, especially in great cities, to help relieve unemployment; such offices have had limited success and are viewed with suspicion by unions because employers may use them during strikes to secure non-union workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off between public employment services and potential strike-breaking uses; effectiveness historically limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation, arbitration, and conciliation boards and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Many states provide for mediation, arbitration, and conciliation: boards may be established (e.g., Massachusetts board established 1886) to which disputes can be submitted in writing with detailed statement and agreement to abide and continue work; boards hear testimony, investigate, and render decisions (often within ten days); boards may initiate investigations but arbitration is not made obligatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards can prevent strikes by facilitating settlement, making public findings to pressure parties, but lack compulsory enforcement power in most states.
